sections.title: The Restrictions and Prohibitions in Eating Meat
sections.html:
As we have learned (in chapter 14), eating meat is a subject that is complex from various aspects. On the one hand, eating it gives a person much strength, physical and emotional, and eating it for the sake of Heaven also has an inner value of tikkun olam (repairing the world). On the other hand, the desire to eat meat can drag a person into craving and cruelty. The rule is that the more vitality, benefit and craving there is in a food, the more mitzvot the Torah added regarding it in order to guide and direct us toward the good side; therefore, regarding eating meat there are more mitzvot and prohibitions.

These are the mitzvot connected with eating meat: 1) Not to eat non-kosher domestic and wild animals, such as the horse and the lion. 2) Not to eat non-kosher birds, such as the ostrich, the eagle and the hawk. 3) Not to eat non-kosher fish, such as the catfish. 4) Not to eat non-kosher locusts. 5) Not to eat sheratzim (creeping creatures) that crawl, fly or live in water, such as the frog, the shrimp and crabs (lobster). 6) To slaughter domestic animals, wild animals and birds. 7) Not to eat their blood. 8) To cover the blood of wild animals and birds. 9) Not to eat the ḥelev (forbidden fat) of domestic animals. 10) Not to eat nevela, an animal that died without sheḥita. 11) Not to eat tereifa, an animal that was slaughtered and found to have a defect in its body. 12) Not to eat ever min ha-ḥai (a limb from a living animal). 13) Not to eat the gid ha-nasheh (sciatic nerve). 14) Not to cook meat with milk, and not to eat such a dish or derive benefit from it (the Rambam, in the introduction to Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot, itemized these mitzvot as 21 mitzvot).

There are mitzvot whose reason is understood, such as the mitzvot of honoring parents, tzedaka and the prohibition of murder; even if these mitzvot were not written in the Torah, it would be proper for us to fulfill them on our own understanding, and these are called mishpatim (ordinances). And there are mitzvot that, had they not been written in the Torah, it would not have occurred to us to fulfill, such as the prohibition of sha'atnez and of eating forbidden foods, and these are called ḥukim (statutes). In a certain respect, the fulfillment of the ḥukim expresses faith and devotion to God more, because we fulfill them only because God, may He be blessed, commanded us so, and not because of any human reason. From this standpoint, we become more sanctified through these mitzvot; accordingly, one should be careful not to find human reasons for these mitzvot that could detract from their sanctified Divine meaning. Similarly the Sages said: "A person should not say: I do not want to eat pork (because it is repulsive), but he should say: I do want to, but what can I do, for my Father in Heaven has decreed thus upon me" (Sifra, Kedoshim 128; Rashi on Vayikra 20:26).

After the fundamental recognition that we are unable to understand the reason for the statutes of the Torah, we may reflect on the values and meanings that we can learn from these mitzvot.

The most important foundation, which is connected to the very fact that these mitzvot are ḥukim, is the separation that these mitzvot create between Israel and the nations. The Holy One, blessed be He, created many animals in the world, and after He permitted human beings to eat the meat of all of them, He separated us from all the nations and sanctified us with His commandments, and permitted us to eat only the kosher species, and forbade us the non-kosher species. As it is stated (Vayikra 20:23-26): "And you shall not walk in the customs of the nation which I am casting out before you, for they did all these things, and I abhorred them. But I said to you: You shall inherit their land, and I will give it to you to possess it, a land flowing with milk and honey; I am the Lord your God, who has separated you from the peoples. You shall therefore separate between the clean animal and the unclean, and between the unclean bird and the clean, and you shall not make yourselves abominable by animal or by bird or by anything that creeps on the ground, which I have separated for you as unclean. And you shall be holy to Me, for I the Lord am holy, and I have separated you from the peoples to be Mine." The Sages said (ibid. in the Sifra): "Just as I am holy, so you be holy; just as I am separate, so you be separate… If you are separated from the nations, you are for My name; and if not, you belong to Nevukhadnetzar king of Babylon and his fellows" (the kings of the nations who subjugated Israel). Thus, before any reason or meaning, the laws of kashrut create a separation between Israel and the nations, and help them preserve their unique identity as the people of God and the heralds of His word to the world.

sections.title: The Kosher and Non-Kosher Species
sections.html:
The Torah divided animals into four categories: 1) domestic and wild animals (mammals); 2) fish; 3) birds; 4) sheratzim (including those that crawl, those that swim in water, and those that fly, among which are the kosher locusts). In all these categories there are kosher species and non-kosher species, as will be explained later in the chapter.

The Torah gave signs to distinguish between kosher and non-kosher animals, fish and sheratzim. It also listed the non-kosher birds, to teach us that the other birds are kosher.

Several of the great Rishonim noted that there is a characteristic trait of the kosher species: they eat grass and have a gentle temperament, whereas the non-kosher species are predators and irascible. And since the food a person eats influences his soul, the Torah commanded that we not eat species that tend toward cruelty (Ramban, Rabbeinu Baḥya and Abarbanel on Vayikra 11; Akeidat Yitzḥak, Shemini, Sha'ar 60).

Some wrote that the kosher species are healthy to eat, whereas the non-kosher species are not healthy (Guide for the Perplexed 3:48). Many objected to mentioning this reason, for it is not proper to diminish the Torah and make it into a book of medicine. Furthermore, we do not find that non-Jews are less healthy in body than Jews; rather, the mitzvot are intended to sanctify Israel and repair their souls, and a Jew who eats forbidden foods defiles his soul, and therefore the Torah called the species that are forbidden to eat "tamei" (impure) (Akeidat Yitzḥak, Shemini, Sha'ar 60; Abarbanel on Vayikra 11).

Likewise, the Sages expounded (Yoma 39a): "Sin dulls a person's heart, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:43): 'Do not make yourselves impure with them, that you should be defiled (ve-nitmetem) by them' – do not read ve-nitmetem but ve-nitamtem (and you will be dulled)." That is, all sins, and especially eating forbidden foods, dull the heart, so that it cannot absorb spiritual matters of holiness. From this aspect, the prohibition of forbidden foods is more severe than other prohibitions, because the forbidden food enters the body, mixes with it and damages it (Ramban, Baḥya, Akeidat Yitzḥak, Abarbanel and Malbim on Vayikra 11).

sections.title: The Signs of Kashrut in Domestic and Wild Animals
sections.html:
The Torah gave two signs for kosher wild and domestic animals, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:2-3): "These are the creatures which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof and is wholly cloven-footed, and chews the cud, among the animals – that you may eat."

The first sign: it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed. A hoof is a hard covering, like a thick nail or soft bone, that grows on the animal's foot, by means of which it treads on the ground without being injured. "Cloven-footed" means that its foot and hoof are split, that is, divided into two parts.

The second sign: it chews the cud. The kosher species, which eat grass, whose digestion is difficult and prolonged, have a special digestive system composed of four stomachs: 1) the rumen (keres); 2) the reticulum (beit ha-kosot); 3) the omasum (ha-masas); 4) the abomasum (keiva). First, the ruminants quickly tear off the grass and chew it a little. From there it descends to the rumen and undergoes initial digestion. From there it passes to the reticulum and forms into small balls. Afterwards it comes back up to the mouth for prolonged chewing, and this is chewing the cud. Afterwards it descends to the omasum and from there to the abomasum.

Four species have one sign in which they resemble the kosher species, but since they do not have both signs of kashrut, they are non-kosher. They are: the camel, the hyrax (shafan), the hare and the pig. As it is stated (Vayikra 11:4-6): "But these you shall not eat, of those that chew the cud or of those that part the hoof." Three of them chew the cud but do not have a cloven hoof, as it is stated: "The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, it is unclean to you. And the hyrax, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, it is unclean to you. And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, it is unclean to you." In practice, the hare and the hyrax do not chew the cud in the usual sense; however, since their mouths appear to be constantly occupied with chewing, like ruminants, and the hare eats its droppings and appears to be chewing the cud, the Torah therefore wrote that they are unclean since they do not part the hoof (Rav David Tzvi Hoffmann, ibid.). The pig parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, and therefore it is unclean, as it is stated (ibid. 7): "And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed, but does not chew the cud, it is unclean to you."

The Sages gave another distinct sign for the kosher species: they have no teeth in the front part of the upper jaw. Another sign: the meat under their tailbone runs crosswise, lengthwise and widthwise. However, the arod (wild ass) also has this sign and it is non-kosher (Ḥullin 59a). They mentioned another sign: the milk of kosher species can curdle into cheese, whereas the milk of non-kosher species does not curdle (Avoda Zara 35a). Another sign was mentioned: anything that has horns is a sign that it is kosher; however, this sign is not agreed upon by all as a definitive sign (Nidda 51b; Ḥullin 59a-b, Tosafot s.v. 'Elu').

In general, the signs that the Torah gave for the kosher species are signs of grass-eaters that are not predators. Since grass is difficult to digest because of the large amount of fiber in it, God created for them an elaborate digestive system and the ability to chew the cud, so that they can continue chewing the food for its digestion. And instead of claws to sink into prey, they have cloven hooves, which are meant to help them run in the mountains and climb rocks, in order to find grass, eat it quickly and flee nimbly from predators to a place where they can chew the food at leisure. The front teeth that they lack in the upper jaw also express the fact that they are not predators, and their teeth are meant for chewing grass. Likewise, the horns are meant for defense and not for attack. Nevertheless, the kosher species manage to survive well in the world, to teach us that if one is willing to make an effort and be content with little, it is possible to find a good livelihood even without preying.

sections.title: The Kosher Species and Their Laws
sections.html:
The Torah listed ten kosher species, as it is stated (Devarim 14:4-5): "These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep and the goat; the ayal, the tzvi, the yaḥmur, the ako, the dishon, the te'o and the zemer." The first three species are behemot, that is, domesticated animals, and the seven species after them are wild animals (ḥayot).

Although regarding the signs of kashrut there is no difference between domestic and wild animals, and all of them are kosher for eating, nevertheless only domestic animals are offered as sacrifices. Following from this, there is a special mitzva regarding domestic animals, that it is forbidden to eat their ḥelev, that is, those fats that were burned from the sacrifices on the altar. On the other hand, there is a special mitzva regarding wild animals and birds, that their blood must be covered with earth after sheḥita (below 18:9-10).

The Sages said (Ḥullin 63b): It is revealed and known before He who spoke and the world came into being that the non-kosher animals outnumber the kosher ones; therefore Scripture enumerated the kosher species. However, like all species in nature, the ten kosher species too branch out into various breeds.

The identity of the three species of domestic animals is known, since they are domesticated species, and therefore their tradition was not forgotten. The first is the ox (shor); in detail, the male is called shor and par, the female para, the young agalim (calves), and the whole family bakar (cattle). There are many breeds of them, among them: Damascus, Holstein, Hereford and Brahma. The second species is the sheep (seh khesavim, or kevasim). The male is called ayil (ram), the female raḥel (ewe), and the young taleh and talya (lambs). Of them too there are many breeds, among them: the fat-tailed sheep, Merino and Awassi. The third species is the goat (seh izim, or izim). The male is called tayish and sa'ir, the female ez and se'ira, and the young gedi and gedia (kids). Of them too there are many breeds, among them: Baladi and Alpine. The two families of sheep and goats together are called tzon (flock).

The identity of the seven species of wild animals was forgotten over the course of the years and the exiles, and now we know with certainty by tradition only two species – the tzvi (gazelle) and the ayal (deer). In practice, however, since the signs of kashrut in domestic and wild animals are clear, every wild animal that has these signs of kashrut is permitted to eat. And so it was ruled in practice regarding the zebu (Kol Mevaser 1:9).

According to the classification accepted today in the science of zoology, all kosher species of domestic and wild animals are in the class of mammals, in the order of 'even-toed ungulates' (Artiodactyla), suborder 'ruminants.' In practice, however, in order to declare a certain species kosher, God-fearing experts must carefully check its signs, and if they are found to be kosher, the species is kosher.1

sections.title: Birds
sections.html:
Regarding birds, the Torah did not write signs of kashrut, but only mentioned the non-kosher species, as it is stated (Devarim 14:11-18): "Every clean bird you may eat. But these are the ones of which you shall not eat: the nesher, the peres, and the ozniya; and the ra'ah, and the ayah, and the dayah after its kind; and every orev after its kind; and the bat ha-ya'ana, and the taḥmas, and the shaḥaf, and the netz after its kind; the kos, and the yanshuf, and the tinshemet; and the ka'at, and the raḥama, and the shalakh; and the ḥasida, and the anafa after its kind, and the dukhifat, and the atalef" (similarly it is stated in Vayikra 11:13-19).

The Sages said (Ḥullin 63b): It is revealed and known before He who spoke and the world came into being that the kosher birds outnumber the non-kosher ones – therefore Scripture enumerated the non-kosher ones, to teach us that all the rest are kosher.

The Sages summarized that there are twenty-four kinds of non-kosher birds, and anyone who recognizes all of them by their names and their signs can determine that all other birds are kosher. However, this tradition was lost over the course of the exile. But the Sages gave several signs for distinguishing between a kosher and a non-kosher bird: every bird that is dores, that is, kills its prey with its claws, is non-kosher. And if one stands it on a string and it divides its feet, two toes on this side and two toes on that side, it is known that it is dores.

Regarding a bird about which it is not known whether it is dores or not: if it has an extra toe, a crop, and its gizzard can be peeled, it is kosher. And if it is known that it is not dores, it suffices that it have one of these three signs to be considered kosher (Ḥullin 59a; Tur, Beit Yosef 82:2; Shakh 4).

In practice, however, the Rishonim wrote that since there were cases in which, on the basis of the signs, a certain bird was thought to be kosher and in the end it turned out that it was dores and non-kosher (see Ḥullin 62b), it is not customary today to rely on the signs, and only a bird about which there is a clear tradition that it is kosher is eaten (Rashi, Rosh, SA and Rema 82:2-3).

Let us mention some of the kosher bird species that are commonly eaten today: the most common is the chicken, and after it the turkey. Some also commonly eat: the domestic goose, the domestic duck, the mute swan, pigeons (the rock pigeon and the large pigeon), the turtledove, the sparrow and the quail.

The commentators explained that since birds are more spiritual than animals, most of their species are kosher. However, it is possible that precisely because they are further from us, their traditions were lost, to the point that in practice only a few of the birds are declared kosher, those about which there is a tradition that they are kosher.

sections.title: Cases of Doubt
sections.html:
When one community has a clear tradition about a certain bird that it is kosher, the other communities may rely on its tradition. This is provided that the tradition of that community is known to be reliable, and that the reason the tradition of this bird's kashrut was preserved only among them is that only in their location was this bird found throughout the years.

But if the members of the communities that were not accustomed to eat that bird had a reason to forbid it – for example, its signs raise a doubt, or they held that the members of the community that were accustomed to eat it were not sufficiently meticulous in transmitting traditions, or because that bird resembles non-kosher birds, and if they eat it there is a concern that they will err and eat non-kosher birds as well – they should continue their custom not to eat that bird (Shakh 82:11, based on the Rosh and Rashba). However, the members of the community that were accustomed to eat it, as long as they have done so with the consent of their rabbis, may continue their custom.

Regarding the turkey, some raised a question: it has been agreed in halakha that only a bird about which there is a tradition from the period of the Mishna that it is kosher may be eaten, whereas the turkey originates from the continent of America, which was discovered in the year 5252 (1492), so there is no tradition about it that it is kosher. And although it has all the signs of kashrut that the Sages listed, there were rabbis who did not want to eat it because there is no tradition about it. In practice, however, it was ruled that it is kosher, and so Jews are accustomed to eat it (Knesset Ha-gedola YD 82:27). Apparently, the first rabbis who saw it held that it is not considered a new species, but rather another breed of chicken, and therefore there is no need for a tradition about it. It is indeed possible that had this question come before other rabbis, they would have tended to be stringent and to consider it a separate species requiring its own tradition. But since the first rabbis who saw it ruled leniently and their ruling spread in many communities, all Jews may eat it. Some say that the turkey should not be forbidden, because only a rare bird is not permitted on the basis of signs and requires a tradition to permit it, since there is a concern that it may sometimes be dores of animals with its claws, and since it is not commonly found among us we have not yet seen this. But when it concerns a bird that is found among us by the thousands, and it is known to all that it is not dores, it may be eaten on the basis of the signs that the Sages listed (Arugot Ha-bosem 16; Meshiv Davar 2:22).

sections.title: Fish
sections.html:
Every fish that has fins and scales is kosher, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:9-11): "These you may eat of all that are in the waters: whatever has fins and scales in the waters, in the seas and in the rivers, those you may eat. And all that do not have fins and scales in the seas and in the rivers, of all that swarm in the waters and of all living creatures that are in the waters, they are an abomination to you. They shall be an abomination to you; you shall not eat of their flesh, and their carcasses you shall hold in abomination" (and likewise in Devarim 14:9-10).

The fin is on the side of the fish and helps it swim. Scales are the covering that grows on the skin of the fish and serves it as an additional shield, with each scale attached on one side to the skin of the fish and on its other side lying on the skin without being attached. It suffices that a fish have one fin and one scale for us to know that it is kosher (Ḥullin 59a; SA 83:1), provided that we know with certainty that the scale was attached to its body and did not fall off another fish and stick to it (Shakh 83:1).

The Sages said: every fish that has scales is known to have fins; thus, in practice, the sign of scales is the determining sign (Ḥullin 66b; SA 83:3).

There are fish that have no scales when they are young, and after a time the scales grow; there are fish that have scales in their youth and afterwards they fall off; and there are fish whose scales fall off when they are brought up from the sea. All these fish are kosher, for any fish that has scales for a certain period of time is a kosher fish (Ḥullin 66a; SA 83:1).

If the scales are very thin, as long as they can be seen with the eye, the fish is kosher. Sometimes, because of their thinness and the color of the fish, it is difficult to see them on it; one can then wrap the fish in a cloth and afterwards examine the cloth: if a scale is found on it, the fish is kosher (Avoda Zara 39a; SA 83:2).

It is the nature of scales that they are attached to the skin of the fish, but their attachment is not very strong, and therefore one can peel them off by hand or with the help of an implement, leaving the skin beneath them intact. But if, in order to remove them, one must cut them and the skin beneath them does not remain intact, this is a sign that they are not scales but part of the skin, and the fish is non-kosher (Rema 83:1). Therefore many forbid the swordfish, because the scales seen on it are part of its skin (see the Harḥavot).

Fish do not require sheḥita, and the prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai does not apply to them. Therefore, it is permitted to cut a limb from them and eat it while they are alive. But to bite into them while they are alive is forbidden, because of the prohibition of 'bal teshaktzu' (do not make yourselves abominable) (Rema 13:1), and because it is a trait of cruelty (Da'at Kohen 12).

sections.title: Locusts
sections.html:
Included in sheretz ha-of (flying creeping creatures), which is forbidden to eat, are all the species that have three pairs of legs and also wings, among them wasps, bees, flies, crickets, the praying mantis and locusts (ḥagavim). Among the locusts, whose characteristic trait is that they leap upon the ground, there are species that are kosher, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:20-21): "All flying creeping things that go upon all fours are an abomination to you. Yet these you may eat of all flying creeping things that go upon all fours: those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to leap upon the earth."

From the Torah we learned two signs of kashrut for locusts: 1) they have two pairs of ordinary legs; 2) kera'ayim – a third pair of large, raised legs intended for leaping. The Sages added, on the basis of tradition, two signs: 3) they have four wings; 4) their wings cover most of their body (Ḥullin 59a).

Even if these signs have not yet grown on the locust, if they will grow on it in the future, it is a kosher species that may be eaten.2

Four kosher species are mentioned in the Torah, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:22): "These of them you may eat: the arbeh after its kind, and the sal'am after its kind, and the ḥargol after its kind, and the ḥagav after its kind." The Sages learned that each of the four has an accompanying species: the one accompanying the arbeh is the tziporet ha-keramim; the one accompanying the sal'am is the yoḥana yerushalmit; the one accompanying the ḥargol is the artzuvia; and the one accompanying the ḥagav is the razbanit (Ḥullin 65a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 1:22).3

Locusts, like fish, do not require sheḥita, and the prohibition of ever min ha-ḥai does not apply to them either. Therefore, it is permitted to cut a limb from them and eat it while they are alive. But to bite into them while they are alive is forbidden, because of the prohibition of 'bal teshaktzu,' and also because it is a trait of cruelty (Da'at Kohen 12). Even to pass it near one's mouth as though about to bite into it is forbidden, because of the prohibition of 'bal teshaktzu,' according to which it is forbidden to do something repulsive (Shabbat 90b; Rema 13:1).

Some say that the general name of all the kosher species is 'ḥagav,' and any species that has the signs of kashrut but whose general name is not ḥagav is non-kosher and forbidden to eat (Ribam, Rosh, Ramban, Rashba, following the view of Rabbi Yosi). Therefore, today locusts are not eaten on the basis of the signs of kashrut alone; rather, there must also be a tradition that its name is ḥagav (SA 85:1). And if there is a tradition about a certain species that it is kosher, it is known that its name is ḥagav.

In recent generations the tradition of permissibility was transmitted in Yemen and Morocco, where locusts are common. The locust that is permitted according to tradition is the species called arbeh, in its various varieties, which sometimes gathers in enormous swarms and destroys all vegetation.4
